extracted.intended_audience: science fiction & fantasy authors, fans, and awards researchers (people interested in Hugo Award rules and history)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, eligibility, and selection process for the Hugo Award for Best Short Story — the WSFS prize for science fiction or fantasy short fiction (award category-level rules and historical notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awarded for (concise definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best science fiction or fantasy story of less than 7,500 words published in the prior calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the category definition used by the Hugo Award for Best Short Story; longer works are eligible in the novelette, novella, and novel categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length eligibility (short story limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short story award is available for works of fiction of fewer than 7,500 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts this length cutoff with other categories (novelette, novella, novel) which cover longer lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Works must be science fiction or fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hugo Awards are given each year for science fiction or fantasy stories published or translated into English during the previous calendar year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and publication-year eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible works are those published or translated into English during the previous calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations to English are eligible (the page notes a translator being credited in 2024); the 'previous calendar year' refers to publication or translation date relative to the award year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection method (voting system and electorate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hugo Award nominees and winners are chosen by supporting or attending members of the annual World Science Fiction Convention (Worldcon) using instant-runoff voting with six finalists (except in the case of a tie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The short stories on the ballot are the six most-nominated by members that year. Ties are an exception to the six-finalist rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination mechanics and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial nominations are made by members in January through March; voting on the ballot of finalists is performed roughly in April through July (timing depends on that year's Worldcon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to 2017 the final ballot contained five works; this was changed in 2017 to six finalists. The page also states there is no limit on the total number of different stories that can be nominated in a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominator limits (post-2017)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the 2017 change, each initial nominator is limited to five nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a constraint on how many works a single supporting/attending member may nominate during the nomination window; it was introduced concurrently with changing the final ballot size to six.

rubrics_metrics.name: No award option
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are permitted to vote 'no award' if they feel that none of the finalists is deserving of the award that year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'no award' receives a majority the Hugo is not given in that category; the Best Short Story category produced a 'no award' result in 2015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retro-Hugo eligibility and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Retro-Hugos are available for works published 50, 75, or 100 years prior, but only for years after 1939 in which no awards were originally given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retro-Hugos have been awarded for specified earlier years (the page lists years such as 1939, 1941, 1943–1946, 1951, and 1954 for short stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical category definition (1960–1966)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1960–1966 the award was titled 'Best Short Fiction' and defined only as a work 'of less than novel length' that was not published as a stand-alone book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During those years both nominees and winners ranged from short story to novella in length because the separate novelette/novella categories were not in the same configuration; the page flags this as an historical exception to the modern 7,500-word cutoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalist record-keeping and ballot size history
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1959 all six candidates have been recorded; the 1955 and 1958 awards did not include recognition of runner-up stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documents historical practice about how many finalists were recorded and how historical inconsistencies are presented in lists of winners/finalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award-year labeling convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The years shown correspond to the date of the ceremony, rather than when the short story was first published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each year entry links to the corresponding 'year in literature' article; readers should note that a story's publication year and the Hugo ceremony year may differ.
